rows.title: Bond sell-off deepens as oil prices rise
rows.content:
Emily Herbert and Ian Smith in London and Kate Duguid in New York

Published September 28 2026

Updated September 28 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

US borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2007 on Monday morning, as fading hopes of a deal between Washington and Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz drove up oil prices.

Brent crude rose more than 4 per cent to a high of $108.83 a barrel, after US President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the strait over the weekend. Oil prices later fell back to around $105.

Renewed selling pressure on US Treasuries sent yields on 10-year bonds up 0.09 percentage points to 5.27 per cent, the highest in nearly two decades. The interest rate-sensitive US two-year yield rose by a similar amount to 4.96 per cent.

“The potential fallout on the global economy from the war with Iran remains a key driver of the macro narrative,” said Ian Lyngen, head of US interest rate strategy at BMO Capital Markets. “There will, eventually, come a point at which the moves in energy will no longer have such an impact on US rates. Clearly, the market has yet to reach such an inflection point.”

UK government bonds also weakened further on Monday, with the 10-year gilt yield rising to 5.44 per cent — its highest level since 2007.

The sell-off on Monday also pushed French and Italian 10-year bond yields to fresh multiyear highs, with French borrowing costs at their highest level since 2008.

The rise in bond yields also weighed on stocks, with the S&P 500 falling 0.5 per cent by midday in New York and the Nasdaq 100 down 0.8 per cent.

US borrowing costs have soared in recent weeks to levels not seen since before the global financial crisis, as signs of persistent inflation and strong growth in the world’s biggest economy have prompted investors to bet on higher interest rates.

The Federal Reserve raised borrowing costs earlier this month for the first time since 2023, and investors in futures markets are betting on two more quarter-point rises by January — a marked shift from the cuts that had been expected before the US-Iran war sent energy prices soaring.

Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chair of research at Barclays, said there was “nothing magical about these yield levels”, and it would take something substantial to reverse the sell-off, such as “if the US economy starts to slow down” or higher rates start “biting” risky assets such as stocks. “That would be one sign that we have perhaps gone far enough.”

Other big central banks are also expected to make a string of rate rises in the coming months to contain a burst of inflation set off by the conflict.

Pooja Kumra, a rates strategist at TD Securities, said the bond sell-off was being powered by a combination of “persistent economic resilience” and the lack of a roadmap to “how the war might be resolved”, which was pushing investors to bet on rates remaining higher for longer.

Paul Watters, head of European credit research at S&P Global Ratings, said: “Our sense is that [bond] yields could grind higher” from here, in part because “we see the energy price shock continuing through 2027”.

“The buffers are eroding” in global energy reserves, Watters pointed out, referring to countries using up their stockpiles.

rows.title: Erdoğan holds rare meeting with Germany’s potential next leader
rows.content:
Anne-Sylvaine Chassany in Berlin

Published September 28 2026

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan met with the man seen as Germany’s chancellor-in-waiting on Monday, compounding the woes of the country’s struggling leader Friedrich Merz.

Hendrik Wüst, premier of Germany’s most populous state, held the unusual meeting with Turkey’s powerful leader during a three-day trip, raising his profile as Merz’s likeliest successor. The presidential meeting — an unusual gesture towards a German regional leader — was announced as Wüst began his trip to Turkey on Monday.

Erdoğan’s willingness to make time for Wüst suggests the crisis engulfing Merz, who has suffered three disastrous recent local election losses , is reverberating beyond the country’s borders.

The 50-minute conversation focused “on the close ties between North Rhine-Westphalia and Turkey, economic co-operation and current political issues”, said a member of Wüst’s delegation.

The Christian Democrat’s trip marks the 65th anniversary of the agreement that allowed hundreds of thousands of Turkish workers to move to West Germany in the 1960s, providing the labour force needed to fuel the country’s postwar “economic miracle”.

Wüst, who leads a coalition of Christian Democrats and Greens in his state, has emerged as a prominent potential successor to Merz, who is battling record-low approval ratings, rising discontent within his party and tensions with his junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats.

A trip by Wüst to Poland in May, which included a visit to Auschwitz, had already prompted speculation in the German media about a possible “chancellor swap” . That speculation turned into a serious debate within the Christian Democratic Union after the far-right Alternative for Germany came first in regional elections in both Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, inflicting severe losses on the party of former chancellors Angela Merkel and Helmut Kohl.

Wüst ventured beyond state issues during his meeting with Erdoğan , with both leaders discussing “Turkey’s importance as a Nato member and strategic partner”, as well as “relations between the European Union and Turkey”. He said afterwards that his state “supports a reform of the EU-Turkey customs union”.

“No region is as closely connected to Turkey, both socially and economically, as North Rhine-Westphalia,” Wüst said in a statement, saluting the “one million people with Turkish roots” living in North Rhine-Westphalia, which is home to 18mn people and the cities of Cologne and state capital Düsseldorf.

But he also expressed his “concern” about “domestic political developments in Turkey”, citing the rule of law and freedom of the press.

The 51-year-old premier, who has no foreign policy experience, also visited German chemicals group Henkel’s plant near Ankara and laid a wreath at the mausoleum of modern Turkey’s founding father Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

Wüst is also due to meet Turkish business executives as he seeks to promote investment in North Rhine-Westphalia and its struggling manufacturing towns. He then plans to travel to Istanbul.

For Erdoğan, the meeting comes as his government battles to contain the fallout of an $18bn financial scandal that has affected more than 450,000 retail investors and prompted the resignation of one of the ruling party’s most senior officials.

The president was due on Monday to lead a cabinet meeting on how to respond to the scandal.

Additional reporting by John Paul Rathbone in Istanbul

rows.title: Five men arrested over alleged RAF Fairford terror plot released on bail
rows.content:
Lucy Fisher and David Sheppard in Liverpool and Charles Clover and Robert Wright in London

Published September 28 2026

Updated September 28 2026

The five British men arrested over a suspected terrorist plot near RAF Fairford have been released on bail in an unexpected development after they were detained by armed police early on Sunday.

Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terror Policing for the UK, said on Monday afternoon that despite being released on bail, the men continued to be suspects.

“They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others,” Taylor said. “They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry.”

The base at Fairford belongs to the UK’s RAF but has been used by the US Air Force to conduct what it classes as defensive strikes on Iran.

Taylor acknowledged the “significant interest” in whether the “current geopolitical context” had a bearing on the incident.

“We are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state,” he added.

The five men, who are all in their twenties, were detained after a local farmer tipped off police early on Sunday morning. They had been held under suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and preparing a terrorist act under the Terrorism Act.

Under the Terrorism Act, officers could have held the men for as long as 14 days before charging them. It is unusual for suspects arrested on suspicion of such serious offences under the Act to be released on bail so quickly.

On Monday, the Iranian embassy in London said it “categorically” rejected and strongly condemned speculation that Tehran was involved in any plan to target RAF Fairford.

Police patrol the perimeter of RAF Fairford on Monday

The incident has raised questions about the extent to which the US and the UK were aware of any threat to the air base, after the witness who tipped off the police said her intervention had been the trigger to stop the alleged attack.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested on Monday morning that the British state may have been aware of the threat, telling Sky News that the farmer had acted “quickly and thoughtfully . . . With respect, though, she does only have a partial picture.”

US President Donald Trump on Sunday said that the authorities had previously been aware of the suspects, as he praised the UK’s response.

“They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great,” he said. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them. Thank you.”

Taylor said he was “very conscious” that there was a great deal of speculation about what might or might not have been known previously about “potential threats or activity”.

He added: “As I hope the public understand, I will not always be able to share this type of information. What I do ask is that the public understand that we work hand in glove with MI5 to keep them safe from a myriad of threats and do everything we can to protect them.”

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told LBC that he would chair a Cobra meeting to discuss the matter later on Monday.

MI5 director Sir Ken McCallum said in an annual update in October last year that over the preceding year there had been more than 20 Iran-backed plots in the UK.

Since then, there have been seven arson and other attacks on Jewish, Israeli and Iranian dissident targets in London claimed by Ashab al-Yamin, a new group closely associated with the Iranian regime.

In July, the UK government said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had “almost certainly directed” those attacks.

Tehran has consistently denied having any hand in that or other attacks in the UK.

The farmer said she had been driving home late from a party when she encountered three vans blocking the road and “saw a large group of hooded and masked men” run off when they spotted her.

She told the BBC’s Today programme that her initial call to the MoD police went unanswered, before she called 999 to alert regular police.

She said she was “staggered” by the official response and accused officials of “dropping the ball” by allowing the alleged terrorist threat so close to the base.

“The air base were operating a roadblock close to the entrance to the base, but not on any of the other roads,” she said. “But we assumed someone would be monitoring the roads around the base perimeter and taking regular patrols in the village. Clearly, this was not happening.”

Additional reporting by Andrew England
